title: The Readout Blind Spot
lesson: A check can miss errors that happen after it finishes.
brief: The gates are relatively reliable, but the final measurements are noisy. Compare a gate-based check with a check that uses the final readout to calculate its syndrome.
learning_moment: A gate-based check finishes before the data qubits are measured. It therefore cannot flag an error that happens only during the final readout. When a check's end edge contains only Z and identity and reaches the final slot, it can be merged into the readout: measured data bits contribute to the syndrome parity. This can make a single readout flip visible to the check without adding end-edge gates. But parity has a blind spot, too: two flips can cancel each other. Compare the Fidelity and Yield of the same check with final readout on and off.
hint: Place one Z check that ends at the last slot. Click it to switch final readout off and on, and test both. Compare the result, not just the Fidelity.
reflection: What readout errors became visible when the check used the final readout? Which errors could still escape?
noise_note: Measurement errors are more likely than gate errors in this puzzle.

explanation: The readout is the noisy part here. A check that ends with gates finishes before the measurement, so it cannot see readout flips.
This Z check on q2 ends at the last slot as Z on q0, q1 and q2, so it uses the final readout: the three measured bits are part of its result. A single readout flip on any of them is caught.
Two flips at once cancel, so a few wrong results still slip through.
